body.text: In Toledo, Ohio, Jeeps are still being made. The assembly plant on the edge of town is open, but the nearby glassworks and steel mills grow quieter each year. For 35 years, Toledo’s families have been promised that life will get better. On November 3, they answered with their votes.

In Ohio’s 9th District, the long-time Democratic representative Marcy Kaptur comfortably beat Republican Derek Merrin, with about 53 per cent of the vote. She kept Toledo even as the country turned against the President. Across the Rust Belt and in regions that had voted Republican for a generation, voters rejected the man they had sent to Washington. What these voters do next, and what the Democrats do with their votes, will shape America until 2028.

Even seasoned observers were surprised. On the Takshashila Institution’s America Votes podcast, political scientist Stephen Farnsworth called it possibly the biggest rejection of a ruling party since Watergate.

Democrats won both Houses of Congress. By November 13, the Associated Press was reporting 255 House seats and 56 Senate seats for the Democrats, including two Independents who caucus with them, with Alaska going blue with Mary Peltola.

In Texas, where Democrats had not won a statewide race since 1994, the party won the governorship and the Senate seat. It also took the state House of Representatives for the first time in 24 years and won the post of Railroad Commissioner, the oil and gas regulator.

Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, its first Democratic governor since 1998 and the first Black woman governor in the country. South Carolina sent a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1998. Ohio, Kansas, and Iowa elected Democratic senators, and Ohio and Iowa also chose Democratic governors.

Even Mississippi, where Democrats had not won a Senate race since 1982, elected Scott Colom, its first Black senator since Reconstruction. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads, with the final ranked-choice count due November 18. Trump won all of these states in 2024. This time, they voted against his party.

The election also brought a generational change. The Senate will have its biggest turnover in nearly 50 years, with at least 15 new members who are, on average, well over a decade younger than those they replace.
Why voters switched

Young voters led the way. Many had supported Trump in 2024, hoping he would fix an economy that felt hopeless to them. This time, they worried about AI taking their jobs, never owning a home, or never being able to retire. Voters under 30 backed Democrats by almost three to one.

The Fox News Voter Analysis found that young men, who favoured Trump by 15 points in 2024, now backed Democrats by 33. Latino voters, who had shifted to Trump in Texas and the Southwest, returned to the Democrats by 27 points nationally in the same survey. They were angered by immigration raids in which, as Farnsworth said, “if you look Latino you could get stopped,” regardless of citizenship.
About seven in 10 voters, including four in 10 Republicans, told the AP Voter Poll that Congress was not doing enough to check the President.

Among those elected were Pia Dandiya, Florida’s first South Asian American in Congress, and Amish Shah, who wrested an Arizona seat from the Republicans. In Ohio, Trump’s pick for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, lost to Democrat Amy Acton.

Democrats chose candidates who matched their districts: evangelicals in rural areas, loggers in logging towns, and workers in working-class ones. Even so, the dominant message was a vote against Trump. Only about half of voters viewed Democrats favourably, and one in five Democratic voters disliked their own party. Asked which party would fight corruption better, a third said neither. Voters removed those in power without showing much trust in their replacements.

Why did voters change their minds so quickly? Two years ago, they gave Trump everything. They knew who he was. They had lived through his first term, watched a mob storm the Capitol and heard the guilty verdicts in a New York court.

Still, they chose him because he spoke about grocery bills and closed factories as if he shared their troubles. Voters gave him both Houses of Congress and a party moulded in his MAGA image, and he already had a Supreme Court that had expanded presidential powers. This time, Trump had no one else to blame, and voters found his government’s failures harder to accept.
Factors that powered the rout

Prices were where voters felt it most. “You simply cannot spin away a price increase,” Farnsworth said. Americans see petrol prices on large roadside signs every day and remember last year’s prices. At the supermarket, their money buys less each week.

Remarks by some Republicans added to the anger. In Mississippi, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, asked about rising beef prices, said Americans who could not afford it had “so many proteins to choose from”. She lost to Scott Colom.

Tariffs meant to bring factories back instead raised prices. Farmers in Kansas paid more for diesel, and truck drivers in Texas paid more for fuel. In the colder northern states, families are worried about the cost of heating oil this winter. For households already skimping on groceries, a single hospital bill can erase a year’s savings.
About two-thirds of voters said Trump’s policies had made the economy worse. Towns like Toledo had been losing ground for 35 years. Trump promised to stop the decline; voters felt it had deepened.

Voters also wanted peace. Trump had promised to end America’s “endless wars” and spend the money at home instead. Rural and small-town families who had sent sons to Helmand in Afghanistan and Fallujah in Iraq felt most strongly about this promise.

What they got was the Venezuela operation, sold to Americans as a quick win that would bring cheaper oil and a friendly government. Nicolás Maduro is now in American custody, but his successor, former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez, runs the same government with the same people.

Then came Iran, a war that all but closed the Strait of Hormuz and pushed up petrol and heating bills across the country. Voters who wanted to end foreign wars found themselves paying for a new one every time they filled their tanks.
The money was the other grievance. Trump came to Washington promising to clean up the capital and “drain the swamp”. His second term has instead seen his family’s wealth grow sharply.

Consider the sons. In 2024, Forbes estimated Eric Trump’s wealth at about $40 million and Donald Trump Jr’s at about $50 million. Eight months into their father’s second term, it put Eric’s at $750 million and Donald Jr’s at $500 million.

They joined company boards and backed drone makers that sell to the Pentagon and Gulf states. They co-founded World Liberty Financial, a crypto company in which a Trump family firm owns 60 per cent. Four days before the inauguration, a UAE-linked company bought nearly half of it for $500 million.

Pakistan signed an agreement to explore using the family’s stablecoin. Its army chief has had lunch at the White House, the first Pakistani army chief to do so who was not also head of state. Jared Kushner’s investment firm manages billions of dollars, mostly from the Gulf, including $2 billion from the Saudi crown prince’s fund, and he reportedly sought more while serving as his father-in-law’s envoy on Iran.

The largest holders of the President’s memecoin were invited to a dinner with him. Qatar gave a Boeing 747 for his use, to pass to his presidential library afterwards. Companies with business before his administration helped pay for a ballroom on the site of the White House’s demolished East Wing.

He pardoned Changpeng Zhao, founder of the crypto exchange Binance, who had pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering programme. Days later, Binance promoted World Liberty’s USD1 stablecoin.

Elon Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to keep the administration’s party in power. By one estimate, the Trump family earned about a billion dollars from crypto alone in a single year. Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts in 2024.

On election day, more than half of voters said corruption was a major factor in their decision, slightly more than said so of the cost of living. “People in government are getting rich off of you,” one political scientist said, “and you can’t get ahead because of that”.
For the man in Toledo, that summed up his life. Under Barack Obama, he had felt looked down on by coastal elites. Now the man who promised to be his voice had joined those same people.
What comes next

In India, a government that lost its majority this badly would fall within days. In Britain, the Prime Minister would go to the palace and resign. In America, Donald Trump woke up on November 4 still President, with two years left in office. Democrats now control both Houses of Congress, but the man voters rejected stays in the White House until January 2029.

To an Indian reader, this system might seem broken. To its founders, it works as intended. After fighting a king, they feared too much power in one person’s hands, and so they split it among the President, Congress and the courts. They further divided powers between Washington (the Centre) and the states. They preferred slow government to one that could turn against the people.

The result does not take effect at once. Until January 3, the old Congress remains in place, and Republicans still run both Houses. Their Senate can still confirm judges the incoming Democrats would reject, though hopes of a Supreme Court retirement that would lock in Republican dominance have faded. Those the voter ousted still hold power for now.
After that, as Farnsworth put it, “When you have divided government, you have the equivalent of a bad marriage”. No one gets along, little is accomplished and everyone waits for the next crisis.

The voter’s anger will find an outlet once the new Congress takes office, because the House will use its powers against the White House. Robert Garcia, the Democrat expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, has already announced his targets: the family businesses he calls the “Trump crime family,” corporations accused of overcharging customers, immigration agents accused of stopping citizens because of their skin colour, and the Epstein files. He has warned administration officials to “lawyer up”. Each of these targets matches a voter grievance.

The House will also control government spending, and no Bill can pass without it. Resolutions on the wars will struggle, because a President can insist that what “smells like a war” and “tastes like a war” is legally not one, as Joshua White of Johns Hopkins University put it on the same podcast. Some Democrats may push for impeachment, but removing a President requires two-thirds of the Senate, which the Democrats do not have. At home, Washington is likely to be deadlocked.

Abroad, things look different. Presidents who do badly in a midterm, White says, “will often pivot more deeply into foreign policy,” where they have more freedom. In war, diplomacy and deals with foreign leaders, Trump retains wide freedom to act. Congress can make it harder, but cannot take foreign policy away from him.

The voter has limited Trump’s power at home but left him free abroad, where countries such as India will feel the effect. For India, White warns, any trade deal will be with “the Trump administration, not with the United States in perpetuity”, and its best course may be to “go hide behind a bush and not be noticed for a while”.
Is the voter betting on the Democrats again? Yes, but cautiously.

The party has two years to prove the voter right, but it can pass little into law while Trump holds a veto. David Plouffe, who managed Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign, says the Democrats should keep passing bills anyway. Vetoes of popular measures on grocery and fuel prices, lapsed health subsidies and tariffs would show voters whose side the President is on, the common man’s or the elite’s.

Plouffe also warns against any talk of impeachment, which cannot succeed in the Senate and would let Trump cast himself as a victim. Hearings on the family business, crypto deals, and ballroom donors would address the voter’s anger more effectively.

Then there are the states. Soon, most Americans will live in states led by Democratic governors. That is where the party can deliver results before 2028: lower power bills, cheaper medicines and homes young families can afford. The Democratic winners in Texas, Kansas and Ohio campaigned on these needs.
If the party returns to the cultural fights that cost it this voter before, it will lose that voter again, as quickly as Trump did. The voter is willing to give anyone only a short chance.

To an Indian reader used to lifelong voting loyalties, the American voter may seem changeable. But this is a voter whose loyalty ended when the factory closed. In 2016, they rebelled against the system and sent Trump to Washington. In 2024, they rebelled against Biden and brought Trump back. In 2026, they have turned against Trump. Three revolts in 10 years: the target changes, but the anger remains.

“American voters are very transactional,” Farnsworth said. “It’s much more a question, over and over again, of what have you done for me lately?” This midterm resembled 2022, when voters punished Biden for high prices. This voter backs whoever promises relief and withdraws support the moment the promise is broken.
“We just don’t think anyone is good enough for us,” Farnsworth said, half-joking. For the man in Toledo, it is no joke. For 35 years, no one has been good enough.
Anil Raman is a retired Army Brigadier who focusses on US politics and foreign policy in the Geostrategy Programme at the Takshashila Institution.
